topic: Car accident? How CTP claims work at our clinic

slides.headline: Car accident? Here's how CTP works
slides.sub: What to bring, who to contact and what happens at your first visit.

slides.title: Step 1: get checked medically
slides.body: After any crash, see your GP, or go to the emergency department if you're worried. Severe neck pain, numbness, weakness, confusion or a bad headache need prompt medical attention before anything else.

slides.title: Step 2: lodge your CTP claim
slides.body: CTP claims go through a compulsory third party insurer, and each state has its own process and time limits. Your GP, the insurer or your state's CTP regulator can explain the steps for you.

slides.title: Step 3: bring your claim number
slides.body: When you book, let us know it's a CTP claim. Bring your claim number, insurer details and any GP referral or certificate. It saves time and keeps the paperwork moving.

slides.title: What we handle for you
slides.body: Once your claim is accepted, we liaise with your insurer or case manager, send the reports they request and keep your treatment documented. The insurer decides what is approved, not us.

slides.title: What recovery usually looks like
slides.body: Most people recover well from common crash injuries like whiplash. Treatment usually focuses on staying gently active, restoring movement and gradually building back to work, driving and exercise.

slides.headline: Questions about your CTP claim?
slides.body: Call or book online and mention it's a CTP claim. Our team can talk you through what to bring and what happens at your first visit.

Been in a car accident and not sure how CTP works? Here's the short version.

topic: Tension headaches and a tight upper back

slides.headline: Headaches that start in your upper back
slides.sub: Why tension headaches and a tight upper back often turn up together.

slides.title: Why the two often go together
slides.body: Tension-type headaches are often described as a band or pressure around the head. Many people also notice tight, tender muscles across the shoulders, upper back and base of the skull when they flare.

slides.title: Move your upper back every hour
slides.body: Long stretches at a desk tend to stiffen the upper back. Sit tall, hands on shoulders, and slowly rotate side to side ten times. Small, regular movement usually beats one big stretch.

slides.title: Check the usual triggers
slides.body: Poor sleep, stress, skipped meals, dehydration and long screen sessions are common contributors. A simple headache diary for two weeks can help you spot patterns you can actually change.

slides.title: Where chiropractic care fits
slides.body: Our chiropractors assess your neck and upper back, may use adjustments or soft tissue work to ease stiffness, and pair that with exercises and habit changes so you're not relying on hands-on care.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See your GP promptly for a sudden, severe headache, one after a knock to the head, headaches with fever, confusion, vision changes, weakness or numbness, or a new pattern that keeps getting worse.

slides.headline: Want a plan for your headaches?
slides.body: Book an assessment with our chiropractors at Hybrid Physiotherapy. We'll look at your neck, upper back and daily habits, and give you a simple routine to start.

caption:
That band-like headache and the tight upper back? They often show up together.

Tension-type headaches are common, and many people notice tender muscles across the shoulders, upper back and base of the skull when they flare. Moving your upper back every hour, keeping an eye on sleep, stress, meals and water, and keeping a two-week headache diary are good places to start.

topic: Back pain after deadlifts: what to change

slides.headline: Deadlifts left your back sore?
slides.sub: Most gym back tweaks settle. Here's what to change in your training.

slides.title: Most gym back tweaks settle
slides.body: A sore back after lifting is common and usually a strain, not damage. Most people improve noticeably within days to a couple of weeks with gentle movement and a few smart training changes.

slides.title: Drop the load, keep the pattern
slides.body: Rather than stopping altogether, keep practising the hinge with a load that feels comfortably light. Staying in the movement pattern tends to help both your confidence and your recovery.

slides.title: Look at your total volume
slides.body: Flare-ups often follow a jump in load, sets or frequency, or a big session on poor sleep. Build back gradually, adding weight over weeks rather than chasing your old numbers straight away.

slides.title: Try a friendlier variation
slides.body: Trap bar deadlifts, block pulls or lighter Romanian deadlifts can feel easier while things settle. Pick the variation you can do with little or no pain, then build from there.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Get checked promptly if pain spreads down the leg with numbness or weakness, you notice changes in bladder or bowel control, or pain is severe, constant and not easing after a week or two.

slides.headline: Want to get back under the bar?
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios assess your lift, your load and your back, then map out a gradual return plan that fits your program.

caption:
Tweaked your back on deadlifts? You probably don't need to stop lifting.

Most gym back pain is a strain, not damage, and it usually settles within days to a couple of weeks. The trick is to keep moving: practise the hinge with a comfortably light load, cut back total volume, and try a friendlier variation like trap bar deadlifts or block pulls while things calm down. Then build the weight back over weeks, not days.

Get checked promptly if pain spreads down the leg with numbness or weakness, if you notice bladder or bowel changes, or if pain is severe and not easing.

topic: Why reformer springs are great for rehab

slides.headline: Why reformer springs help in rehab
slides.sub: Adjustable support and adjustable challenge, all on one machine.

slides.title: Springs can assist or resist
slides.body: On a reformer, springs can make a movement harder or help you through it. That means someone early in rehab can practise a movement with support, then gradually take that support away.

slides.title: Load you can adjust in small steps
slides.body: Changing a spring changes the load in small, predictable steps. For rehab, that makes it easier to build up gradually rather than jumping from bodyweight straight to heavier gym weights.

slides.title: Lying down takes pressure off
slides.body: Many reformer exercises are done lying or seated, so you can train legs, hips and trunk without full bodyweight through a sore knee, hip or back. Useful early on, then progress to standing.

slides.title: Control through the whole range
slides.body: Springs keep tension on through the movement, including the return. Controlling that return, rather than letting the carriage snap back, builds strength and control in positions you use every day.

slides.body: Our Pilates team starts with an assessment, then sets springs and exercises for your goals and progresses them as you improve. Health fund cover depends on your fund and policy, so check with your fund.

topic: Mid-back pain from long drives

slides.headline: Long drive, stiff mid-back?
slides.sub: Simple changes for the car, and what to do when you get out.

slides.title: Why long drives stiffen you up
slides.body: Hours in one position, a fixed arm reach and road vibration can leave the mid-back feeling stiff and achy. It's usually about staying still for too long, not damage to your spine.

slides.title: Set up the seat first
slides.body: Sit back fully in the seat, bring it close enough that your elbows stay softly bent, and tilt the backrest slightly back from upright. A small rolled towel behind your lower back can help.

slides.title: Break it up every two hours
slides.body: Road safety advice already suggests a break every two hours. Use it well: walk for a few minutes, reach your arms overhead, squeeze your shoulder blades back and gently rotate each way.

slides.title: Where chiropractic care fits
slides.body: If stiffness keeps coming back, our chiropractors can assess your mid-back and neck, use adjustments or soft tissue work where appropriate, and give you mobility exercises to use between drives.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See a doctor promptly if mid-back pain comes with chest pain, shortness of breath, fever or unexplained weight loss, follows a crash or fall, or is constant and worse at night.

slides.headline: Stiff after every road trip?
slides.body: Book with our chiropractors at Hybrid Physiotherapy. We'll assess what's going on, use hands-on care where it helps and send you off with a few simple exercises.

caption:
Hours behind the wheel and your mid-back feels like a plank of wood?

Long drives keep you in one position with a fixed reach and constant vibration. The stiffness that follows is usually about stillness, not damage. Start with your seat: sit right back, elbows softly bent, backrest tilted slightly back, and a rolled towel behind your lower back if it helps.

Then use the two-hourly break road safety advice already recommends. Walk for a few minutes, reach overhead, squeeze your shoulder blades back and gently rotate each way.

topic: Sleep and pain: why a bad night makes everything hurt more

slides.headline: Slept badly? That's why everything hurts
slides.sub: Sleep and pain feed each other. Here's how to break the loop.

slides.title: Sleep changes how pain feels
slides.body: Research suggests even one poor night can make the nervous system more sensitive, so the same sore back or knee feels louder the next day. It's not in your head, and it's not new damage.

slides.title: Pain and sleep feed each other
slides.body: Pain makes it harder to sleep, and poor sleep turns pain up. The good news is that improving either side of that loop, even a little, often helps the other side too.

slides.title: Protect a steady routine
slides.body: Aim for a similar bedtime and wake time most days, get daylight early, and keep caffeine to the morning. A wind-down routine without screens for the last half hour can help too.

slides.title: Get comfortable, not perfect
slides.body: There's no single right sleeping position. Use pillows to support sore spots, like one between the knees for side sleepers or under the knees on your back. Choose whatever lets you settle.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See your GP if pain wakes you every night and doesn't ease with changing position, comes with fever, sweats or weight loss, or if snoring, gasping or ongoing insomnia are wearing you down.

slides.headline: Pain keeping you up at night?
slides.body: Our Sunnybank and Milton physios can assess what's driving your pain, help you move with more confidence and build a plan that works alongside better sleep.

caption:
Ever noticed your back hurts more after a rough night? You're not imagining it.

Research suggests poor sleep can make the nervous system more sensitive, so the same niggle feels louder the next day. Pain then makes sleep harder, and round it goes. The good news: nudging either side of the loop often helps the other.

Try a steady bedtime and wake time, morning daylight, caffeine before lunch and a screen-free wind-down. Use pillows to get comfortable rather than chasing a perfect position.

See your GP if pain wakes you every night and doesn't change with position, comes with fever or weight loss, or if snoring or ongoing insomnia are wearing you down.

topic: Trigger points: what those tight knots actually are

slides.headline: What are those tight knots, really?
slides.sub: Trigger points explained, without the myths.

slides.title: Myth: knots are tangled muscle
slides.body: Those tender spots aren't balls of tangled muscle or trapped toxins. Researchers still debate exactly what trigger points are, but they're generally described as sensitive areas in a muscle that feel tight and ache.

slides.title: Why they refer pain elsewhere
slides.body: Pressing a spot in your upper shoulder and feeling it up your neck is common. The nervous system shares signals between nearby areas, so where you feel it isn't always where it's coming from.

slides.title: What tends to make them flare
slides.body: Long hours in one position, sudden jumps in training, stress and poor sleep are common contributors. They often show up in the upper shoulders, neck, lower back and around the hips.

slides.title: What massage can and can't do
slides.body: Remedial massage can ease tenderness and help you feel looser for a while. Research suggests the effects are usually short term, so it works well alongside movement, not instead of it.

slides.title: Keep the benefit going
slides.body: After a session, move the area gently, break up long sitting with short walks and build strength gradually. Regular movement tends to keep those spots calmer than waiting for the next massage.

slides.headline: Want those knots looked at?
slides.body: Book with our remedial massage therapists at Hybrid Physiotherapy. We'll work on the tender areas and suggest simple movements to keep things feeling easier.

caption:
Those tight knots in your shoulders aren't tangled muscle or trapped toxins.

Trigger points are generally described as sensitive, tender spots in a muscle, and researchers still debate exactly what's going on in them. Pressing one can send an ache somewhere nearby, which is why a spot in your shoulder can feel like it's in your neck. Long hours in one position, training spikes, stress and poor sleep often make them grumpier.

Remedial massage can ease that tenderness and help you feel looser for a while. The effects are usually short term, so keep moving afterwards: gentle movement, short walks between sitting and gradual strength work help keep things calm.

topic: Heat or ice: which one and when

slides.headline: Heat or ice? A simple way to choose
slides.sub: Neither is magic, but each has a place. Here's when to use which.

slides.title: Ice: fresh knocks and sprains
slides.body: For a new sprain or bump in the first couple of days, a cold pack can take the edge off pain. Wrap it in a cloth and keep it to about 10 to 15 minutes at a time.

slides.title: Heat: stiff and achy muscles
slides.body: For stiffness, ongoing back or neck ache, or tight muscles, warmth often feels more soothing. A heat pack or warm shower before moving can make it easier to get going.

slides.title: Honestly, pick what feels good
slides.body: Current guidelines suggest neither heat nor ice speeds healing much on its own. They're comfort tools. If one helps you move more easily, that's a good enough reason to use it.

slides.title: Movement does the heavy lifting
slides.body: Whatever you choose, pair it with gentle movement within comfort. Walking, easy range of motion exercises and a gradual return to normal activity usually matter more than the pack itself.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Get checked if you can't take weight on the injured limb, there's major swelling or an odd shape, numbness or colour change, or pain after a heavy fall. Avoid heat or ice on numb skin.

slides.headline: Not sure what you've done?
slides.body: Our Milton and Sunnybank physios can assess it, explain what's going on and give you a clear plan for the next few weeks.

caption:
Heat or ice? The honest answer: it matters less than you think.

As a rough guide, ice suits fresh knocks and sprains in the first couple of days. Wrap it and keep it to 10 to 15 minutes. Heat tends to suit stiffness, ongoing aches and tight muscles, especially before you get moving.

Current guidelines suggest neither one speeds healing much on its own. They're comfort tools, so use whichever helps you move more easily, and pair it with gentle movement and a gradual return to normal activity.

topic: Pilates for runners

slides.headline: Runner? Here's what Pilates adds
slides.sub: Strength and control for the bits running doesn't train much.

slides.title: Running is repetitive loading
slides.body: Every run is thousands of similar steps. Most running niggles come from doing more than your body is ready for, so building strength and capacity alongside your running makes a lot of sense.

slides.title: Single-leg strength and control
slides.body: Running is basically hopping from one leg to the other. Reformer and mat work for hips, glutes and calves helps you control each landing, especially as you tire late in a run.

slides.title: Trunk control, not a rigid core
slides.body: You don't need a rock-hard core to run well. Pilates trains your trunk to stay steady while your arms and legs move, which is exactly what running asks of it. Breathing gets trained too.

slides.title: Fitting it into your week
slides.body: One or two sessions a week is a good starting point. Slot them on easy days or rest days, and avoid a hard session the day before a long run or race.

slides.title: Clinical Pilates, not a class
slides.body: Our Pilates team assesses how you move and your running history, then builds a program you can progress. Health fund cover for clinical Pilates varies, so check with your fund.

slides.body: Book a clinical Pilates assessment at Hybrid Physiotherapy. Bring your running goals and we'll build a program around your training.

topic: Massage before or after a race or big event

slides.headline: Timing your massage around race day
slides.sub: How to plan it so it helps, not hinders.

slides.title: Nothing new in race week
slides.body: Race week isn't the time to try a deep tissue massage for the first time. If massage is already part of your routine, stick with what you know works for your body.

slides.title: Before: go lighter, go earlier
slides.body: If you like a pre-event massage, book it two to four days out and ask for lighter pressure. Deep work close to a race can leave you feeling sore or flat on the day.

slides.title: After: wait a day or two
slides.body: Straight after a big event, rest, rehydrate, eat and walk it out. A gentle massage a day or two later can help you feel less stiff. Save deeper work for later in the week.

slides.title: Set realistic expectations
slides.body: Research suggests massage can reduce how sore you feel after exercise, but it doesn't replace sleep, food, easy movement or a sensible return to training. Think of it as one helpful piece.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Sharp pain that stops you running, swelling, pain on one specific spot of bone, or calf pain with warmth and swelling need a proper assessment by a physio or GP, not a massage.

slides.headline: Got an event coming up?
slides.body: Book with our remedial massage therapists at Hybrid Physiotherapy. Tell us your event date and we'll plan pressure and timing around it.

caption:
Massage before a race or after it? Timing matters more than you'd think.

Race week isn't the time to try deep tissue work for the first time. If you like a pre-event massage, book it two to four days out and keep the pressure lighter. Deep work too close to the start line can leave you feeling flat.

topic: Your flare-up plan: what to do in the first 48 hours

slides.headline: Your 48-hour flare-up plan
slides.sub: A simple timeline so you're not guessing when pain spikes.

slides.title: First: flare-ups are common
slides.body: A flare-up is a spike in pain, and it's not usually a sign of new damage. Most settle within a few days, especially if you keep moving gently and try not to panic.

slides.title: Hours 0 to 12: calm it down
slides.body: Ease off whatever set it off, but avoid lying in bed all day. Try comfortable positions, slow breathing, and heat or ice if it helps. Short walks around the house count.

slides.title: Hours 12 to 24: little and often
slides.body: Do short bouts of gentle movement often, like a few minutes of walking every hour or easy range of motion exercises. Aim for movement that feels okay rather than pushing through sharp pain.

slides.title: Hours 24 to 48: build back up
slides.body: Start reintroducing normal tasks at a reduced dose, like shorter desk blocks or half your usual walk. Most people notice things easing by now, even if it's not all the way there.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Get checked if pain is severe and not easing after a couple of days, spreads down a limb with numbness or weakness, or comes with fever, unexplained weight loss, or bladder or bowel changes.

slides.headline: Want a flare-up plan of your own?
slides.body: Our Sydney CBD and Chatswood physios can build a personal flare-up plan with you, so you know exactly what to do next time.

caption:
Flare-ups feel less scary when you already know what to do.

A flare-up is a spike in pain, usually not new damage, and most settle within a few days. In the first 12 hours, ease off whatever set it off but avoid bed rest: comfortable positions, slow breathing, heat or ice if it helps. From 12 to 24 hours, move little and often. From 24 to 48 hours, bring normal tasks back at a reduced dose.

topic: Stiff lower back after a long flight

slides.headline: Long flight, stiff lower back?
slides.sub: What to do in the air and in the first day after landing.

slides.title: Why flights stiffen you up
slides.body: Hours sitting in a cramped seat with little room to shift can leave your lower back stiff and achy. It's usually about stillness, not damage, and it often eases within a day or two.

slides.title: In the air: move every hour
slides.body: Get up for a short aisle walk when it's safe. In your seat, try pelvic tilts, gentle knee lifts and ankle circles. A rolled jumper behind your lower back can help too.

slides.title: Handle cabin bags in two steps
slides.body: Wheel bags where you can, and lift cabin luggage close to your body in two steps: onto the seat, then into the locker. Heavy overhead lifts at an awkward angle tend to provoke sore backs.

slides.title: After landing: walk it out
slides.body: Resist collapsing onto the hotel bed. A 10 to 20 minute walk, a warm shower and a few gentle back stretches usually help things loosen up more than resting all day.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Get checked promptly if back pain comes with leg weakness, numbness around the groin, or bladder or bowel changes. Calf pain with swelling or sudden breathlessness after a flight needs urgent care.

slides.headline: Still stiff days after landing?
slides.body: Book with our chiropractors at Hybrid Physiotherapy. We'll assess your lower back, use hands-on care where it helps and give you exercises to keep moving.

caption:
Landed with a lower back that feels welded in place? Very common after a long flight.

Hours in a cramped seat with little chance to shift usually means stiffness, not damage. In the air, take a short aisle walk when it's safe, and try pelvic tilts, knee lifts and ankle circles in your seat. Lift cabin bags in two steps, close to your body.

After landing, go for a 10 to 20 minute walk and a warm shower before you rest. It usually helps more than lying down all day.

topic: Pilates after knee or hip surgery

slides.headline: Pilates after joint surgery: where it fits
slides.sub: How clinical Pilates can support rehab after knee or hip surgery.

slides.title: Your surgeon's guidance comes first
slides.body: Every surgery and surgeon is a bit different. Instructions on weight bearing, movement limits and timelines come first, and clinical Pilates is planned around them, not instead of them.

slides.title: Why the reformer suits early rehab
slides.body: Springs can support part of your bodyweight, so you can practise squats, bridges and leg presses with less load than standing. Load is then increased in small, controlled steps.

slides.title: What sessions often focus on
slides.body: Common goals include regaining range of motion, rebuilding strength around the hip, thigh and calf, improving balance and getting confident with stairs, getting out of the car and walking further.

slides.title: Expect a gradual build
slides.body: Recovery after joint surgery usually takes months, not weeks. Some soreness after sessions is common. Your program is adjusted as you progress, so each stage feels challenging but manageable.

slides.title: When to contact your surgeon
slides.body: Contact your surgeon or GP promptly for increasing redness, heat or discharge at the wound, fever, calf pain or swelling, sudden breathlessness, or a big change in pain or ability to bear weight.

slides.headline: Planning your rehab after surgery?
slides.body: Book a clinical Pilates assessment at Hybrid Physiotherapy. Bring your surgeon's notes and we'll build a program that fits your stage of recovery.

topic: There is no perfect posture

slides.headline: There's no such thing as perfect posture
slides.sub: Why your next position matters more than your current one.

slides.title: Myth: bad posture causes pain
slides.body: Research suggests there's no strong link between how people sit or stand and whether they get back or neck pain. People with all kinds of posture live without pain, and the reverse is true too.

slides.title: Fact: staying still is the issue
slides.body: Holding any position for hours, even a textbook one, tends to get uncomfortable. Your body likes variety, so changing position regularly usually helps more than holding one 'correct' shape.

slides.title: Slouching isn't dangerous
slides.body: Slumping on the couch or leaning on your desk is not harming your spine. If it feels comfortable, it's fine. If it starts to ache, treat that as a friendly nudge to move.

slides.title: Try the 30-minute nudge
slides.body: Set a gentle reminder every 30 minutes to shift position, stand, stretch or refill your water. Mix sitting, standing and moving through the day instead of chasing one ideal pose.

slides.title: Strength beats straightness
slides.body: Building general strength and fitness helps your body tolerate long days at a desk. Regular walks, a couple of strength sessions a week and activities you enjoy go a long way.

slides.headline: Desk days leaving you sore?
slides.body: Our Chatswood and Sydney CBD physios can look at what's actually driving your pain and help you build a simple plan that fits your workday.

caption:
Sitting up straight all day won't protect your back. Here's why.

Research suggests there's no strong link between posture and back or neck pain. Plenty of people with 'bad' posture have no pain, and plenty with 'good' posture do. What does tend to bother us is staying in one position for too long, even a textbook one.

So slouching on the couch is fine. If it starts to ache, take that as a nudge to move. Set a 30-minute reminder to shift, stand or walk, and build general strength and fitness so your body handles long desk days more easily.

topic: Desk shoulders: tight upper traps and what helps

slides.headline: Shoulders up around your ears by 3pm?
slides.sub: What's going on with tight upper traps, and what helps.

slides.title: Tight often means tired
slides.body: Your upper traps run from the base of your skull to your shoulders. After long desk days and stress, that tight feeling often means muscles tired from working for hours, not muscles that are too short.

slides.title: Three desk resets to try
slides.body: Roll your shoulders slowly backwards five times. Drop your shoulders and lengthen your neck for three breaths. Then shrug up hard, hold two seconds and let go completely. Repeat through the day.

slides.title: Build some shoulder strength
slides.body: Rows, shrugs and overhead presses done a couple of times a week can help the area handle long days better. Start light, and add load gradually over a few weeks.

slides.title: Where remedial massage fits
slides.body: Remedial massage can ease tenderness and help the area feel looser for a while. It works well alongside movement breaks and strength work rather than on its own as the whole plan.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: See a GP or physio if neck or shoulder pain comes with pins and needles, numbness or weakness in the arm, severe headaches or dizziness. Chest pain or breathlessness needs urgent care.

slides.headline: Shoulders feeling like concrete?
slides.body: Book with our remedial massage therapists at Hybrid Physiotherapy. We'll work on the tight spots and show you a few resets to use at your desk.

topic: Which service is right for my problem? A simple guide

slides.headline: Physio, chiro, Pilates or massage?
slides.sub: A simple guide to where to start, and why it's not a big decision.

slides.title: Physio: injuries and rehab
slides.body: Physiotherapists assess and treat injuries, pain and movement problems, from sprains and sore backs to rehab after surgery. Expect a thorough assessment, hands-on care where useful and a clear exercise plan.

slides.title: Chiro: spine, neck and joints
slides.body: Chiropractors assess and treat back, neck and joint problems. Care may include adjustments, soft tissue work and exercise, with adjustments used as one tool among several rather than the whole plan.

slides.title: Clinical Pilates: build strength
slides.body: Clinical Pilates is supervised exercise on reformers and mats, tailored after an assessment. It suits people returning from injury or surgery, managing ongoing pain or wanting to build strength and control.

slides.title: Remedial massage: ease tension
slides.body: Remedial massage therapists work on tight, tender muscles and stiffness. It can help you feel looser and move more comfortably, and works well alongside exercise rather than replacing it.

slides.title: Still unsure? That's fine
slides.body: Many problems can be helped by more than one approach. Our practitioners work under one roof and refer to each other, so if a different service suits you better, we'll point you there.

topic: Calf strain in tennis and pickleball players

slides.headline: Calf strains on court, explained
slides.sub: Common in tennis and pickleball. Here's the usual road back.

slides.title: Why the calf goes on court
slides.body: Quick push-offs, lunges and stop-start movement put heavy load through the calf. Strains often happen late in a match, early in the season or after a jump in how much you play.

slides.title: The first few days
slides.body: Ease off, but keep walking comfortably if you can. Shorter steps or a small heel raise in your shoe may help. Gentle ankle movements and calf raises within comfort usually start early.

slides.title: Build calf capacity gradually
slides.body: Progress from double-leg to single-leg calf raises, then add weight, speed and small hops over the following weeks. Your calf needs to handle far more load than walking before court time.

slides.title: Returning to the court
slides.body: Most people return within a few weeks, depending on severity. Start with hitting drills and short, easy games before competitive matches, and keep calf strength work going in the background.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Get checked if you can't walk or rise onto your toes, felt a sudden kick to the back of the heel, or have calf swelling, warmth and redness without a clear injury.

slides.headline: Calf keeping you off the court?
slides.body: Our Sunnybank and Milton physios will assess the strain, map out a return plan and get you back playing when it's sensible.

caption:
Felt a sharp grab in your calf mid-rally? You're in good company.

topic: Carrying kids and bags on one side

slides.headline: Always carry on the same side?
slides.sub: Kids, bags and shopping: small swaps that spread the load.

slides.title: One-sided carrying is normal
slides.body: Most of us have a favourite hip for a toddler and a favourite shoulder for a bag. It's not harmful, but doing it for hours every day can leave one side feeling tired and achy.

slides.title: Swap sides on purpose
slides.body: Try switching hips or shoulders at each doorway, or every few minutes on a walk. It feels awkward at first, but giving your usual side a break often makes a noticeable difference.

slides.title: Change the carry, not just the side
slides.body: Front carriers, backpacks with both straps on and shopping split into two even bags all spread the load. Hold kids close to your body rather than perched out on one hip.

slides.title: Build strength for the job
slides.body: Carrying is a lifting task, so train it. Farmer's carries, suitcase carries with a bag in one hand, squats and rows a couple of times a week can help your body handle daily loads.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: Get checked if pain spreads down an arm or leg with numbness or weakness, keeps waking you at night, or isn't easing after a few weeks despite changes to how you carry.

slides.headline: Sore from the daily carry?
slides.body: Book with our chiropractors at Hybrid Physiotherapy. We'll assess your back, neck and shoulders, use hands-on care where it helps and give you exercises for daily lifting.

topic: Breathing in Pilates: why it matters

slides.headline: Holding your breath through the hard bit?
slides.sub: Why breathing is part of every Pilates exercise.

slides.title: Breath and effort are linked
slides.body: Most people hold their breath when a movement gets hard. It feels like it helps, but it often adds tension through the neck and jaw and makes the exercise harder to control.

slides.title: The basic pattern
slides.body: A common cue: breathe in to prepare, then breathe out through the hardest part of the movement. It's a starting point rather than a strict rule, and your instructor may adapt it for you.

slides.title: Breathe into your ribs
slides.body: Place your hands on your lower ribs and breathe so they widen sideways and slightly back. This lets you keep gentle tummy tension while still taking a full, comfortable breath.

slides.title: Use the out-breath
slides.body: A slow, steady out-breath often makes it easier to feel your deep abdominal and pelvic floor muscles switch on. Try it before a bridge or leg lift and notice the difference.

slides.title: Try this today: five slow breaths
slides.body: Lie on your back, knees bent, hands on your ribs. Breathe in through the nose for about four counts and out through the mouth for six. Five rounds before bed is a good start.

slides.headline: Want to learn it properly?
slides.body: Our clinical Pilates team starts with a one-on-one assessment and coaches your breathing into every exercise, at a pace that suits you. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Holding your breath through the hard part of a Pilates exercise? You're not alone.

Breathing isn't just a nice extra in Pilates. Most people brace and hold their breath when a movement gets hard, which often adds tension through the neck and jaw and makes control harder, not easier.

A simple starting point: breathe in to prepare, breathe out through the hardest part. Let your lower ribs widen sideways as you breathe in, and use a slow out-breath to feel your deep tummy and pelvic floor muscles switch on.

Try five slow breaths lying down tonight: in for four, out for six. It's a small habit that carries into every session.
